Empirical Research Plan – “Economic Growth and Forest Cover in Developing Countries”

────────────────────────────────────────
1. IDENTIFICATION STRATEGY
────────────────────────────────────────
Chosen method: Two–stage least squares (panel IV) with a Bartik (shift–share) instrument.

Rationale  
• We observe GDP growth, not an on/off “treatment.”  
• Global, plausibly exogenous commodity‐price shocks in world markets create large, differential income shocks across countries depending on their pre-existing export mix.  
• These shocks are externally driven (institutional context) and thus satisfy the spirit of the question (“variations … driven by external factors”).  
• The panel dimension (≈ 20–25 yrs × ~50 countries) plus country and year fixed effects absorb unobserved heterogeneity and common shocks.

────────────────────────────────────────
2. TREATMENT AND CONTROL
────────────────────────────────────────
Treatment variable (endogenous): ΔGDPpc_it  = log(GDP per‐capita)_it  –  log(GDP per‐capita)_{i,t-1}

Instrument (Z_it): Σ_k  (export share of commodity k in country i in base year 1980) × (global price growth of k in t)  
• Continuous; “high-Z” country/years receive larger exogenous growth shocks.  

Control / counterfactual: Country–years with low predicted growth from the instrument serve as implicit controls in the 2SLS framework.

Timing: Annual observations; the instrument varies each year with world prices but export shares are fixed at their 1980 values to ensure exogeneity.

(We do not employ an RDD, so no running variable or cutoff.)

────────────────────────────────────────
3. KEY IDENTIFYING ASSUMPTIONS
────────────────────────────────────────
A1. Relevance: Commodity-price shocks significantly affect GDP growth in exporting countries.  
 Plausibility: Strong historical correlation; F-stat > 10 in similar studies.

A2. Exclusion: Conditional on controls, commodity price shocks affect forest cover only through their impact on aggregate income (not directly).  
 Plausibility: Reasonable for broad commodity baskets; we will drop wood & pulp prices and control for mining value added to reduce direct channels.

A3. Pre-determined shares: 1980 export shares are not chosen in anticipation of future forest outcomes.  
 Plausibility: 1980 is safely pre-period for most satellite coverage.

A4. SUTVA / no cross-country spillovers: A price shock for one exporter does not directly change another’s forests except through the common price (captured by year FE).  
 Plausibility: Acceptable at annual frequency.

A5. Linear additivity & homogeneous LATE: The IV estimates the average causal response among countries whose growth responds to the instrument.  
 Plausibility: Standard in shift-share settings; interpretation restricted to complier group.

────────────────────────────────────────
4. MAIN THREATS & MITIGATION
────────────────────────────────────────
T1. Direct effect of commodity booms on land-use (e.g., mining, oil pipelines).  
 – Drop extractive commodities most likely to clear forest.  
 – Control for mineral rents (% GDP).  
 – Run leave-one-commodity-out robustness.

T2. Endogenous export structure (shares may evolve).  
 – Fix weights at 1980; alternative spec.: weights averaged 1975-85.  
 – Show robustness to different base years.

T3. Differential trends in forest policy / governance correlated with commodity dependence.  
 – Country FE absorb level differences.  
 – Interact region dummies with linear time trend.  
 – Add time-varying controls: democracy index, forest protection laws, aid for conservation.

────────────────────────────────────────
5. R CODE OUTLINE (executable)
────────────────────────────────────────
```r
# Packages
library(tidyverse)
library(fixest)      # fast felm / iv
library(lmtest)      # coeftest
library(sandwich)    # vcovHC

# 1. Load data --------------------------------------------------------------
df <- read_csv("growth_forest_panel.csv") # assume wide panel

# 2. Variable construction --------------------------------------------------
df <- df %>%
  arrange(country, year) %>%
  group_by(country) %>%
  mutate(
    ln_gdp_pc     = log(gdp_per_capita),
    d_gdp_pc      = ln_gdp_pc - lag(ln_gdp_pc),
    forest_pct    = forest_area_pct,               # already %
    d_forest_pct  = forest_pct - lag(forest_pct)
  ) %>% ungroup()

# Build shift–share instrument
price_vars   <- grep("^price_", names(df), value = TRUE)       # global prices
share_vars   <- grep("^share80_", names(df), value = TRUE)     # 1980 export shares

# instrument = Σ share80_k * Δln(price_k)
df <- df %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  mutate(
    bartik = sum(c_across(all_of(share_vars)) *
                 c_across(all_of(price_vars)), na.rm = TRUE)
  ) %>% ungroup()

# 3. Main 2SLS regression ---------------------------------------------------
feols_main <- feols(
  d_forest_pct ~ 1 | country + year | (d_gdp_pc ~ bartik),
  data = df,
  vcov = "hetero"
)
summary(feols_main)

# 4. Robustness: drop extractive commodities -------------------------------
extractives <- c("share80_oil", "price_oil", "share80_minerals", "price_minerals")
df_rb <- df %>% select(-all_of(extractives))

feols_rb <- feols(
  d_forest_pct ~ 1 | country + year | (d_gdp_pc ~ bartik),
  data = df_rb,
  vcov = "hetero"
)
summary(feols_rb)
```

────────────────────────────────────────
6. EXPECTED RESULTS
────────────────────────────────────────
Theory suggests that higher income in low-income agrarian countries raises demand for land-intensive activities (crops, livestock, infrastructure), so forest cover is likely to fall.  
Prior: A 1-percentage-point increase in annual GDP-per-capita growth reduces forest cover by roughly 0.05–0.10 percentage points per year (elasticity ≈ –0.05 to –0.10).

────────────────────────────────────────
7. VALIDITY CHECKLIST SELF-ASSESSMENT
(1 = clearly satisfied, 0 = questionable)
────────────────────────────────────────
C1: Instrument relevance (F-stat > 10) …… 1  
C2: Exclusion restriction …………………… 0.5  
C3: No spillovers (SUTVA) ………………… 0.8  
C4: Monotonicity / well-defined LATE …… 0.8  
C5: Balance / pre-trend diagnostics …… 0.9  

Average score: 0.8 – methodology is strong but hinges on exclusion.
